title: Home Fire Extinguishers: How to Choose, Place, Check, and Use Them (ABC Ratings + PASS)
question: What kind of fire extinguisher should I get for my house, where should I put them, and how do I know if mine still works?
summary: For most homes, buy a UL-listed rechargeable multipurpose ABC extinguisher for each floor plus the kitchen and garage, and mount each one near a room's exit — not under the sink or right beside the stove, where a fire can block the one tool you need. The mistake most people make is buying a single cheap disposable unit, hiding it, and never checking the gauge; a quick monthly glance (needle in the green) and replacing or recharging after any use is what actually keeps it working. When a fire starts, the rule is get everyone out and call 911 first — only fight a small, fully contained fire with a clear escape route behind you, using PASS: Pull, Aim low, Squeeze, Sweep.

commonCauses.cause: Wrong or missing extinguisher for the location — one unit for the whole house, or a 'kitchen' can that is only rated B:C and useless on ordinary paper/wood fires
commonCauses.quickCheck: Read the rating on the label; general living areas want a multipurpose 'A:B:C' unit rated at least 2-A:10-B:C, and you should have at least one per floor plus the kitchen and garage

commonCauses.cause: Extinguisher is discharged or expired and nobody noticed
commonCauses.quickCheck: Look at the pressure gauge — the needle must sit in the green band — and find the date stamp; if it is roughly 10-12+ years old (NFPA 10 pulls non-rechargeable units at 12 years from manufacture) or the needle is in the red, it is not reliable

commonCauses.cause: Mounted in a bad spot, such as under the sink or right next to the stove, where a fire blocks access to it
commonCauses.quickCheck: Stand at the room's exit — can you grab the extinguisher on your way out without reaching over or through where a fire would be? If not, it is in the wrong place

commonCauses.cause: Dry-chemical powder has caked or settled into a solid brick and will not spray properly
commonCauses.quickCheck: Lift and gently shake the extinguisher; if the powder feels like a solid slug that thuds instead of shifting, it needs professional service or replacement

commonCauses.cause: No one in the household knows PASS or when NOT to fight a fire
commonCauses.quickCheck: Ask each capable household member to explain PASS and the 'get out and call 911 first' rule; confirm the pin and tamper seal on each unit are still intact

fixes: Buy the right types: at least one UL-listed RECHARGEABLE multipurpose ABC extinguisher (metal valve head), rated at least 2-A:10-B:C — a common 5-lb home unit is usually rated higher, around 3-A:40-B:C — for main living areas and the garage; add a smaller 5-B:C or 1-A:10-B:C unit for the kitchen and one for each car. Rechargeable (metal head) beats disposable (plastic head) because you can service it.
Cover the whole home: place a unit on every floor/level, in or just outside the kitchen, in the garage, and near sleeping areas. A common target is one per floor plus one for each high-risk room.

Mount each one on its wall bracket along your escape path so you grab it while moving toward the door — never in a spot that could trap you behind the fire. Keep the kitchen unit near the exit, NOT under the stove or sink.

Set mounting height so the handle is within easy reach — NFPA 10 puts the top of a unit under 40 lb no more than 5 feet above the floor, with the bottom at least 4 inches up — and keep it visible and unobstructed. Use a stud finder or wall anchors so the bracket reliably holds the weight.
Register the unit with the maker, read the manual, and write the purchase date plus a replacement date on the body with a permanent marker so nobody has to guess later.

Do a monthly visual check: needle in the GREEN band, pull-pin and tamper seal intact, nozzle and hose clear and uncracked, body free of dents/rust/corrosion, and label legible. For dry-chemical units, if the manufacturer recommends it, gently invert and tap or shake to keep the powder loose.

After ANY use on a rechargeable unit — even a one-second burst — take it to a fire-equipment service company to recharge, or replace it. A partly discharged extinguisher can fail the next time you need it.

Replace disposable (plastic-head, non-rechargeable) units the moment the gauge leaves green, and in any case by 12 years from the date of manufacture — NFPA 10 requires non-rechargeable units be taken out of service then, since they cannot be recharged or tested. Have rechargeable units professionally serviced, internally examined (about every 6 years), and hydrostatically pressure-tested (about every 12 years) on the NFPA 10 schedule, and replace any unit at the manufacturer's stated end of life.

Teach PASS to everyone old enough to use it: PULL the pin (breaks the seal), AIM low at the BASE of the fire (not the flames), SQUEEZE the lever slowly, and SWEEP side to side. Stand about 6-8 feet back — a home unit empties in only ~8-20 seconds.

Make the household rule explicit: on any fire, get everyone out and call 911 FIRST. Only fight a fire if it is small and contained, you have the right extinguisher, the room is not filling with smoke, and your escape route is behind you — and leave instantly if it does not go out fast or the extinguisher empties. Never try to put out a fire fed by a gas line or a strong gas smell, or one that has spread to walls or the ceiling — get out, call 911, and call the gas utility from outside.

Rehearse the kitchen grease-fire drill separately: turn OFF the burner and slide a metal lid over the pan to smother it. Never use water or flour and never carry the burning pan; reach for the extinguisher only if the lid fails and you are between the fire and the exit. Pair all of this with working smoke alarms and a written escape plan.
diyVsPro: Choosing, buying, mounting, doing the monthly gauge check, and using an extinguisher are all DIY — no license needed. Call a licensed fire-equipment service company for the parts that require equipment and certification: recharging a rechargeable unit after any use, the internal examination (about every 6 years) and hydrostatic pressure test (about every 12 years) required by NFPA 10, and the annual inspection/tagging your local fire code may require for rental properties, HOAs, or home businesses. And the clearest line of all: any fire beyond a small, fully contained one — and any fire fed by gas or that has reached the walls/ceiling — is a 911 job for the fire department, not a DIY fight. Get out.
typicalCostUSD: DIY: a 5-lb rechargeable multipurpose ABC unit runs about $40-70; a small 5-B:C kitchen/car unit about $15-25; a full home set of 3-4 units roughly $120-250. Pro service: recharging a used unit about $15-40 plus any parts, and a hydrostatic test about $20-45 per unit.
timeEstimate: About 1-2 hours to buy and mount a set for the whole home; roughly 5 minutes per unit for the monthly gauge check.
safetyNote: The real hazard here is fire and smoke, which spread and incapacitate within minutes — the most dangerous mistake is trying to fight a fire you should flee. Get everyone out and call 911 FIRST; only fight a small, fully contained fire when you have the right extinguisher and a clear escape route behind you, and leave the instant it does not go out quickly or the unit empties — never turn your back on a fire. Grease fire: turn off the heat and cover the pan with a metal lid — never throw water or flour and never carry the burning pan (water flashes the hot oil into a fireball; flour can flash or dust-explode). Electrical fire: never use water; use a C-rated (ABC) extinguisher and cut power at the switch or breaker only if you can reach it safely. Gas-fed fire or a strong gas odor: do NOT try to extinguish it — get everyone out and call 911 and your gas utility from outside, because killing the flame while gas keeps flowing lets it build up and can cause an explosion. Dry-chemical residue is a respiratory and eye irritant, so ventilate and clean up after any discharge, and always recharge or replace a unit after use. This guide does not replace your local fire department or the manufacturer's instructions.
toolsParts: UL-listed rechargeable multipurpose ABC dry-chemical extinguisher (metal valve head, at least 2-A:10-B:C) for living areas and garage
Smaller 5-B:C or 1-A:10-B:C extinguisher for the kitchen and each vehicle
Optional Class K wet-chemical extinguisher if you do a lot of deep-frying
Wall mounting bracket / hanger (usually included with the unit)
Drill with appropriate screws and wall anchors
Permanent marker to date the unit
Metal pan lid kept near the stove for smothering grease fires
Working smoke alarms on every level and near bedrooms
Written home fire escape plan with two ways out of each room
Owner's manual and NFPA 10 inspection guidance
